LCC: Groups the physical things that cover the ground surface, such as buildings, bare rock, plants and water, regardless of what people use the land for.
LCC-1: Surfaces without plants, either built by people (e.g. roads, buildings) or made of natural materials like rock, sand or soil.
LCC-1_1: Places where people have replaced the natural ground with built structures or artificial materials, e.g. towns, roads and industrial sites. Urban parks and other greenery are not counted here.
LCC-1_1_1: Ground covered by buildings or by hard surfaces such as concrete, asphalt or paving that water cannot soak through, e.g. houses and pavements.
LCC-1_1_1_1: Permanent roofed structures that shelter people, animals or goods, or house production and services, e.g. homes, barns or factories.
LCC-1_1_1_1_1: Ordinary medium or large buildings where people live, work or do business, e.g. houses, blocks of flats, offices, shops, farm buildings and factories.
LCC-1_1_1_1_2: Buildings of notable size, height or shape that stand out as landmarks, e.g. stadiums, churches, towers or large greenhouses.
LCC-1_1_1_2: Free-standing human-made structures that are not buildings, e.g. bridges, chimneys, pylons, storage tanks, pipelines or solar panels.
LCC-1_1_1_3: Flat ground covered with a hard surface like asphalt or concrete that water cannot soak through, e.g. paved roads, car parks, squares and airport runways.
LCC-1_1_2: Human-made surfaces that are not paved or built on and still let water soak through, e.g. gravel areas or dumped waste, though plants may still struggle to grow.
LCC-1_1_2_1: Flat open areas surfaced by people with loose or compacted material that still lets water through, e.g. gravel squares, crushed stone, earth sports fields or grass pavers.
LCC-1_1_2_2: Ground covered by discarded material such as household or industrial waste, e.g. construction rubble, slag, scrap metal or wood.
LCC-1_2: Bare surfaces made of natural materials kept in their natural form, whether or not people have affected them, e.g. rock, sand or soil.
LCC-1_2_1: Natural solid stone surfaces with no plant cover, forming a continuous hard layer that lets little water through, e.g. exposed bedrock.
LCC-1_2_1_1: Exposed solid rock with only a few cracks or small patches of soil, e.g. rock outcrops, fresh lava flows or quarry faces.
LCC-1_2_1_2: Soil surfaces that have hardened permanently through chemical or physical processes, forming a crust that water and plant roots cannot get through.
LCC-1_2_2: Ground made of loose mineral particles of any size, laid down by nature or by people, e.g. beaches, sand dunes, scree slopes or river gravel banks.
LCC-1_2_2_1: Loose pieces of rock produced as larger rock breaks down over time and then piled up by nature or people; further split by particle size.
LCC-1_2_2_1_1: Large rock pieces, roughly 20 to 200 cm or bigger, too heavy for people to carry far and moved only by gravity, glaciers or major floods.
LCC-1_2_2_1_2: Medium-sized rock pieces between about 2 and 20 cm, moved and piled up by erosion, e.g. scree on mountain slopes or gravel river banks.
LCC-1_2_2_1_3: Small loose grains between 0.06 mm and 2 cm that wind and water can shift, e.g. sand dunes, sandy beaches or volcanic ash.
LCC-1_2_2_1_4: Very fine mineral particles smaller than 0.06 mm that wind and water can easily move, e.g. muddy river banks or fine volcanic ash.
LCC-1_2_2_1_5: A jumble of unsorted rock material ranging from fine dust to large boulders, most often debris left behind by glaciers.
LCC-1_2_2_2: Soil that could support plants because it holds enough mineral and organic matter, but has no plant cover when observed, e.g. a freshly ploughed field.
LCC-1_2_2_3: Natural material that builds up over time, either as minerals left when water evaporates or as plant remains that have not fully rotted, e.g. salt crusts or peat.
LCC-1_2_2_3_1: Mineral layers left behind when water evaporates, such as salt or gypsum, e.g. the crust on a dried-out salt lake.
LCC-1_2_2_3_2: Layers of partly rotted plant material, mostly bog moss, that build up in waterlogged wetlands where lack of oxygen slows decay.
LCC-2: Any ground covered by plants, whether wild, semi-natural or planted by people, e.g. forests, crops or city parks; subdivided by plant type.
LCC-2_1: Plants with stems made of wood that survive from year to year, such as trees and shrubs; leaf type and whether they lose their leaves are recorded separately.
LCC-2_1_1: Long-lived woody plants with a single main trunk that branches out, e.g. oaks, pines, fruit trees or ornamental trees. Giant bamboo is not included.
LCC-2_1_2: Woody plants with several stems growing from at or near the ground, usually under 5 metres tall, e.g. hawthorn or juniper.
LCC-2_1_2_1: Ordinary shrubs with several stems from the base and an open, spreading shape, usually under 5 metres tall, e.g. hedgerow bushes.
LCC-2_1_2_2: Very low woody plants, usually no taller than 25 cm, that thrive in harsh alpine, arctic or dry places, e.g. heather, bilberry or rosemary.
LCC-2_2: Non-woody plants whose above-ground parts die back at the end of the growing season and regrow from roots, bulbs or seeds, e.g. grasses and wildflowers.
LCC-2_2_1: Grasses and grass-like plants with narrow leaves growing from the base, including true grasses, sedges and rushes, whether wild or farmed, e.g. lawns, meadows or cereal crops.
LCC-2_2_1_1: Wild or cultivated grass-like plants that do not grow taller than about 2 metres, e.g. meadow grasses, sedges, rushes or wheat. Reeds and bamboo are not included.
LCC-2_2_1_1_1: Members of the true grass family, wild or cultivated, e.g. pasture grasses, lawn turf, or cereals such as wheat, barley and maize.
LCC-2_2_1_1_2: Sedges and rushes, grass-like plants often found in marshes, wet meadows and other damp places, e.g. cotton grass or soft rush.
LCC-2_2_1_2: Tall grass-like plants that can grow higher than 2 metres, e.g. common reed, tall bamboo species or sugar cane.
LCC-2_2_2: Non-woody plants that are not grasses, such as wildflowers, ferns and many farm crops, e.g. sunflowers, vegetables, strawberries or hops.
LCC-2_3: Plants that store water in thick leaves, stems or roots to survive dry or salty conditions, e.g. cacti, stonecrops or glasswort on salt marshes.
LCC-2_4: Small, simple plant-like organisms such as lichens, mosses and algae, which grow on rocks, soil, tree bark or in water.
LCC-2_4_1: Crusty, leafy or bushy growths formed by a fungus living together with algae or bacteria, e.g. the grey-green patches on rocks and tree bark.
LCC-2_4_2: Small, non-woody plants only a few centimetres tall, without true roots, that take in water and nutrients mainly through their leaves, e.g. bog moss.
LCC-2_4_3: A large, varied group of simple plant-like organisms that mostly live in or near water, though some grow on damp rocks or tree trunks.
LCC-2_4_3_1: Large algae with branching, leaf-like shapes that can grow several metres long, rooted underwater or floating, e.g. seaweed or kelp.
LCC-2_4_3_2: Tiny single-celled or small clustered algae, usually living in water as plankton but also as green films on rocks or tree trunks.
LCC-3: Surfaces covered by water in any form, either liquid (e.g. rivers, lakes, sea) or frozen (snow and ice).
LCC-3_1: Water in its liquid form, whatever its shape, saltiness or origin, in a fairly stable bed, e.g. rivers, lakes or the sea. Areas only briefly flooded are not included.
LCC-3_1_1: Inland water surfaces not directly connected to the open sea, whether fresh or salty, natural or human-made, e.g. rivers, lakes and reservoirs.
LCC-3_1_1_1: Flowing water such as rivers, streams, creeks or canals.
LCC-3_1_1_2: Still, non-flowing water, mainly lakes and ponds, e.g. natural lakes, fishponds, reservoirs or cut-off river bends (oxbow lakes).
LCC-3_1_2: Sea water on the seaward side of the average high-tide line, including tidal flats along coasts that flood and drain with the tides.
LCC-3_2: Water in frozen form, such as snow, ice and glaciers.
LCC-3_2_1: Ground covered by snow, e.g. snowfields on high mountains that remain all year.
LCC-3_2_2: Ground covered by ice, including glaciers formed as snow piles up and compacts into ice over many years.
LUA: Groups the ways people use land, such as farming, industry, services, transport or housing. An area can carry several uses, recorded at the most detailed level known.
LUA-1: Land used to produce goods directly from local natural resources, e.g. farming, forestry, fishing, mining and quarrying, plus nearby first-stage processing.
LUA-1_1: Land used to grow crops or raise animals for food, sale, own use or industry, including greenhouses, fallow fields and biofuel crops.
LUA-1_1_1: Fields, orchards and grasslands farmed to produce crops or fodder for people, livestock, bioenergy or industry, in the open or in greenhouses.
LUA-1_1_2: Buildings and facilities on farms, e.g. farmhouses, animal sheds, manure stores and buildings for handling or processing crops.
LUA-1_1_2_1: Farm facilities for housing and feeding livestock, e.g. cattle sheds, poultry houses or pig barns; also covers insects and land snails.
LUA-1_1_2_2: Farm areas or buildings used for storage, e.g. barns or maize silage clamps.
LUA-1_1_2_3: Farm facilities other than animal housing or storage, used for handling and processing crops and similar tasks, e.g. a grain drying or sorting shed.
LUA-1_1_3: Land where people grow food or keep animals for their own household rather than for sale, e.g. kitchen gardens or private animal sheds.
LUA-1_2: Land used to grow and harvest wood, e.g. timber, firewood or pulpwood, including tree nurseries and log storage areas, in natural or planted forests.
LUA-1_3: Land used to extract naturally occurring materials such as coal, ores, gravel, sand, salt, oil, natural gas or peat, above or below ground.
LUA-1_4: Areas used for commercial fishing and for farming fish and other water animals.
LUA-1_4_1: Areas used to breed and rear fish and other water animals, e.g. fish hatcheries, mussel farms or crocodile farms.
LUA-1_4_2: Water areas used for commercial catching of wild fish and seafood, typically offshore.
LUA-1_5: Primary production not covered by farming, forestry, mining or fishing, e.g. commercial hunting, gathering wild products, herding migratory animals or beekeeping.
LUA-1_5_1: Areas, fenced or open, used for professional hunting of wild animals.
LUA-1_5_2: Areas used for keeping and feeding animals that roam over large ranges, such as reindeer or deer.
LUA-1_5_3: Areas where wild, uncultivated products other than wood are gathered for sale, e.g. wild berries, mosses or lichens.
LUA-1_5_4: Areas used for honey production, with one or more bee colonies present; like hunting, its outer boundary is often hard to draw.
LUA-2: Land used by industry to turn raw materials into finished or part-finished goods, e.g. factories, plus their linked storage and transport areas.
LUA-2_1: Groups factory-based production of goods, split into raw materials industry, heavy products and light products.
LUA-2_1_1: Industry that turns farm, forest and mining output into basic manufactured materials, e.g. sawmills, steelworks or chemical plants.
LUA-2_1_1_1: Sites used for preparing and spinning fibres, weaving fabric, making thread, and tanning or dressing leather, e.g. a textile mill.
LUA-2_1_1_2: Sites that process wood into products, e.g. sawmills and plants making plywood, fibreboard, joinery, cork or straw goods.
LUA-2_1_1_3: Sites used for making pulp, paper, cardboard, paper-based hygiene products or wallpaper, e.g. a paper mill.
LUA-2_1_1_4: Sites used for producing coke, refining petroleum or processing nuclear fuel, e.g. an oil refinery.
LUA-2_1_1_5: Sites making chemicals and synthetic fibres, e.g. fertilisers, paints, medicines, soap, glue or nylon. Natural fibres like cotton or flax are not included.
LUA-2_1_1_6: Sites used for producing, processing and casting iron, steel and other metals, and for making metal products, e.g. a steelworks or foundry.
LUA-2_1_1_7: Sites making glass, bricks, ceramics, cement, concrete, lime or plaster, or cutting and shaping stone, e.g. a brickworks.
LUA-2_1_1_8: Sites used for making tyres, tubes, plastic packaging and other rubber or plastic goods.
LUA-2_1_1_9: Sites producing basic manufactured materials that do not fit any of the other raw industry categories.
LUA-2_1_2: Industry that turns basic manufactured materials into heavy finished products such as machinery and vehicles.
LUA-2_1_2_1: Sites making machines for industry, farming, forestry and other uses, as well as weapons, ammunition and household appliances (but not vehicles or aircraft).
LUA-2_1_2_2: Sites building vehicles and transport equipment, e.g. car factories, shipyards, or plants making aircraft, trains, motorcycles or bicycles.
LUA-2_1_2_3: Sites making heavy finished products that do not fit the machinery or vehicle categories.
LUA-2_1_3: Industry that turns basic manufactured materials into lighter consumer goods, e.g. food, clothing, electronics or furniture.
LUA-2_1_3_1: Sites that process food, drinks and tobacco, e.g. meat and dairy plants, flour mills, breweries or animal feed factories.
LUA-2_1_3_2: Sites making clothing, fur and leather goods, luggage, bags, saddles and footwear.
LUA-2_1_3_3: Sites used for publishing and printing books, newspapers and journals, and for producing copies of sound recordings.
LUA-2_1_3_4: Sites making electrical, electronic and precision equipment, e.g. computers, cables, batteries, lamps, phones, medical instruments or watches.
LUA-2_1_3_5: Sites making other light consumer goods, e.g. furniture, jewellery, musical instruments, sports goods and toys.
LUA-2_2: Land used to produce electricity or heat, e.g. power stations, wind farms or solar parks.
LUA-2_2_1: Land where nuclear power plants are operated.
LUA-2_2_2: Power plants that burn fossil fuels such as coal, oil, natural gas or peat.
LUA-2_2_2_1: Power plants that burn coal or lignite (brown coal) to generate energy.
LUA-2_2_2_2: Power plants that burn mineral oil to generate energy.
LUA-2_2_2_3: Power plants that burn natural gas to generate energy.
LUA-2_2_2_4: Power plants that burn peat or other fossil fuels not covered by the coal, oil or gas categories.
LUA-2_2_3: Power plants that burn fuels made from plants or organic matter, e.g. wood, biogas or other biofuels.
LUA-2_2_4: Land used to produce energy from renewable sources other than biomass, e.g. hydropower, solar, wind, geothermal, tidal or wave power.
LUA-2_2_4_1: Areas that generate electricity by letting river currents or water falling from reservoirs turn turbines, e.g. hydroelectric dams. Tidal power is not included.
LUA-2_2_4_2: Areas that collect sunlight to produce electricity or heat using solar panels or solar heat collectors, on land or floating on water.
LUA-2_2_4_3: Areas on land or offshore that generate electricity with wind turbines, e.g. a wind farm.
LUA-2_2_4_4: Areas that produce heat or electricity using the natural heat from deep underground, e.g. a geothermal power station.
LUA-2_2_4_5: Coastal areas that generate electricity by using tidal currents to turn turbines.
LUA-2_2_5: Areas where energy is produced by burning waste, e.g. a waste-to-energy incinerator.
LUA-2_5: Land used to make industrial products that do not fit any of the other industry or energy categories.
LUA-3: Land used to provide services to businesses and the public, e.g. shops, offices, hotels, schools, hospitals, government buildings and leisure facilities.
LUA-3_1: Land used to provide commercial services, such as shops, real estate, hotels and restaurants.
LUA-3_1_1: Land used for buying and selling goods wholesale or retail and for repairing vehicles and household items, e.g. shops, car dealers or repair workshops.
LUA-3_1_2: Land used for real estate and renting services, e.g. estate agency or property rental offices.
LUA-3_1_3: Land used for places to stay and eat, e.g. hotels, holiday villages, campsites, restaurants, bars and canteens.
LUA-3_1_4: Commercial services not covered elsewhere, e.g. beauty salons, spas or other wellbeing services.
LUA-3_2: Land used to provide financial, professional or information services, typically in offices.
LUA-3_2_1: Land used for banking, lending, insurance and other financial services, e.g. bank branches or insurance offices.
LUA-3_2_2: Land used for expert services such as IT, research and development, law, accounting, architecture, engineering, advertising or consulting.
LUA-3_2_3: Land used for media and communication services, e.g. publishing, film and TV production, radio broadcasting, post, telecoms and data processing.
LUA-3_2_4: Land used for support services to businesses and people, e.g. travel agencies, rental firms, cleaning or security companies.
LUA-3_2_5: Financial, professional or information services that do not fit any of the other categories in this group.
LUA-3_3: Land used to provide services to the community, e.g. public administration, schools, hospitals and religious sites.
LUA-3_3_1: Land used for government administration, defence, courts, police, fire services and compulsory social security, e.g. town halls or military bases.
LUA-3_3_2: Land used for education at all levels, from primary schools to universities and adult education.
LUA-3_3_3: Land used for health care and social work for people and animals, e.g. hospitals, clinics, care homes or veterinary practices.
LUA-3_3_4: Land used for religious purposes, e.g. places of worship, monasteries and cemeteries.
LUA-3_3_4_1: Buildings for religious worship of any faith, e.g. churches, mosques or synagogues, including their associated administrative buildings.
LUA-3_3_4_2: Monasteries, where a community of people lives together to devote their lives to practising their religion according to set rules and rituals.
LUA-3_3_4_3: Burial grounds of any faith, including historical cemeteries.
LUA-3_3_5: Land used for community services not covered by the other categories, e.g. cemeteries.
LUA-3_4: Land used for culture, entertainment, sport and recreation, e.g. museums, theme parks, stadiums and city parks.
LUA-3_4_1: Land used for arts, libraries, museums, zoos, botanical gardens, historical sites and other cultural services.
LUA-3_4_1_1: Indoor venues for culture, e.g. libraries, museums and theatres.
LUA-3_4_1_2: Outdoor places for culture, e.g. zoos and botanical gardens.
LUA-3_4_2: Land used for entertainment, e.g. amusement parks, theme parks and casinos or other gambling venues.
LUA-3_4_3: Land used for sports facilities, e.g. stadiums, sports halls, swimming pools, gyms, ski resorts and golf courses.
LUA-3_4_3_2: Prepared slopes used for alpine skiing, snowboarding and other snow sliding sports.
LUA-3_4_3_3: Outdoor tracks for racing, e.g. motor racing circuits, motocross or mountain bike courses, horse racecourses and skate parks.
LUA-3_4_3_4: Indoor halls big enough for team ball games such as basketball, volleyball or handball.
LUA-3_4_3_5: Sports grounds (grass, sand, artificial turf, etc.) surrounded by covered or open stands for spectators, e.g. a football stadium.
LUA-3_4_3_6: Indoor swimming halls and outdoor swimming pools.
LUA-3_4_3_7: Outdoor sports fields without a roof or spectator stands around them, e.g. a local football pitch or athletics track.
LUA-3_4_3_8: Indoor gyms and clubs for fitness and individual sports such as boxing, wrestling, body workouts or gymnastics, smaller than full sports halls.
LUA-3_4_3_9: Harbours for leisure boats and yachts, covering the land areas and, where relevant, the harbour water itself.
LUA-3_4_4: Outdoor areas used for leisure, from city parks and playgrounds to national parks and countryside such as forests, moors, lakes and mountains.
LUA-3_4_4_1: Green spaces in towns used for leisure, e.g. city parks, playgrounds and other urban greenery.
LUA-3_4_4_2: Natural or near-natural areas used for leisure, e.g. national parks, forests, heaths, mountains, lakes or rivers used for walking and recreation.
LUA-3_4_5: Recreational uses not covered by the other culture, entertainment and recreation categories, e.g. allotments or hobby fishing.
LUA-3_4_5_1: Small plots of land in towns rented as gardens, sometimes for growing food but mainly for leisure.
LUA-3_4_5_2: Ponds, lakes, rivers and nearby land used for hobby fishing, mainly inland. Offshore fishing is not included.
LUA-3_5: Land used for services that do not fit any of the other service categories.
LUA-4: Land used for the basic networks society depends on, e.g. transport, storage, communications, water supply and sewage or waste treatment.
LUA-4_1: Land used for transport infrastructure, such as roads, railways, airports and ports.
LUA-4_1_1: Land used for road transport, e.g. roads, car parks and service stations.
LUA-4_1_2: Land used for rail transport, e.g. tracks, railway stations and rail yards.
LUA-4_1_3: Land used for air transport, e.g. airports and their related services.
LUA-4_1_4: Land and water used for shipping and boat transport, e.g. ports, docks and navigable rivers.
LUA-4_1_5: Land used for forms of transport that do not fit the road, rail, air or water transport categories.
LUA-4_2: Land used to store industrial or trade goods away from factory sites, plus the facilities that support this, e.g. warehouses and distribution centres.
LUA-4_3: Land used for public services that keep a place running, such as power and water supply, sewage handling and waste treatment.
LUA-4_3_1: Areas used to deliver energy, such as electricity lines, gas networks and district heating, including pipelines that carry oil and gas.
LUA-4_3_1_1: Land used to move electricity to users, e.g. the corridors of power lines and the sites of electrical substations.
LUA-4_3_1_2: Land used to distribute gas to users, e.g. gas pipeline routes and their associated stations.
LUA-4_3_1_3: Land used to distribute heat to buildings, e.g. the pipes and facilities of a district heating network.
LUA-4_3_2: Areas used to supply clean water and deal with sewage, from extraction and purification to storage, distribution and wastewater treatment, pipelines included.
LUA-4_3_2_1: Facilities and their grounds for getting, treating, storing and distributing drinking water, e.g. a waterworks or a water reservoir site.
LUA-4_3_2_2: Sites where wastewater from homes and businesses is cleaned before release, e.g. a municipal sewage treatment plant.
LUA-4_3_2_3: Basins built to hold back runoff water in a stream so that the risk of flooding downstream is reduced.
LUA-4_3_2_4: Ponds kept in ski resort areas to store water that is used for making artificial snow.
LUA-4_3_2_5: Basins that store water for putting out fires or for watering farmland, and sometimes forest land.
LUA-4_3_3: Areas where waste is collected, treated or recycled, e.g. landfills, incinerators, composting sites and hazardous waste plants.
LUA-4_3_3_1: Areas where waste is collected and deposited, such as a landfill or rubbish tip.
LUA-4_3_3_1_1: Waste that can harm people or nature and needs special handling or sealed sites. What counts as hazardous depends partly on national law.
LUA-4_3_3_1_2: Waste that poses no danger to people or the environment, e.g. construction rubble and normal household rubbish.
LUA-4_3_3_2: Sites where used materials are prepared for reuse, e.g. paper, plastic bottles and glass, or garden waste turned into compost.
LUA-4_3_4: Land used for utility services that do not fit into the energy, water, sewage or waste categories.
LUA-5: Land used mainly for people's homes, from city apartment blocks to rural houses and mobile homes, including areas mixed with compatible uses.
LUA-5_1: Housing areas where people live all year round, e.g. detached houses with gardens, terraced rows or blocks of flats.
LUA-5_2: Housing areas mixed with other uses that sit well alongside homes, e.g. local shops, services or light workshops.
LUA-5_3: Housing that is not a permanent main residence, such as holiday cottages, temporary camps or informal settlements.
LUA-5_3_1: Solid buildings used only part of the year as homes, e.g. summer cottages or holiday houses.
LUA-5_3_2: Areas of temporary shelters that are not built to last, e.g. refugee camps or camps for migrant people.
LUA-5_3_3: Settlements built outside any legal or planning framework, such as slums or favelas, that over time become quasi-permanent.
LUA-6: Land that fits none of the main use groups (production, services, transport and utilities, housing), including areas under construction.
LUA-6_1: Land where building work is currently under way. Used for actual present use, not for future planned use.
LUA-6_3: Land left in a natural state with no economic use, e.g. untouched wilderness or remote mountain areas.
LUA-6_4: Land set aside to reduce flooding, e.g. a polder that can be flooded on purpose to lower a river's flood peak.
LCH: Groups extra descriptive details that can be attached to land cover or land use, such as materials, plant traits, water conditions, status, patterns, shape and timing.
LCH-1: Details that describe built-up areas, such as how much ground is sealed, building layout, construction materials, green roofs and transport features.
LCH-1_1: Measures the share of an area covered by sealed, waterproof surfaces like asphalt, concrete or buildings, given as a percentage (%).
LCH-1_2: Groups the typical ways buildings are sized and spread across an area, from scattered farmhouses to dense city blocks.
LCH-1_2_1: A few buildings spread out with clear gaps between them, not dominating the landscape, as in sparsely populated countryside.
LCH-1_2_2: Large multi-storey buildings standing apart with open space between them, housing many people or offices, e.g. apartment blocks or a skyscraper.
LCH-1_2_3: Suburban housing where gardens take up much of each plot, e.g. rows of terraced or semi-detached houses.
LCH-1_2_4: City-centre blocks enclosed by streets, with buildings standing wall to wall along the street and mostly paved backyards.
LCH-1_2_5: Very large stand-alone buildings or halls, e.g. a football stadium, airport terminal, train station or cathedral.
LCH-1_3: Groups labels for what kind of building something is, based on the INSPIRE buildings standard, e.g. church, silo, lighthouse or greenhouse.
LCH-1_3_1: A value naming the specific type of a building, taken from the INSPIRE buildings code list, e.g. chapel, tower or windmill.
LCH-1_4: Groups labels for man-made structures that are not buildings, e.g. bridges, dams, chimneys, pylons, wind turbines or solar panels.
LCH-1_4_1: A value naming the type of a non-building structure, taken from an INSPIRE code list, e.g. antenna, retaining wall or storage tank.
LCH-1_5: Groups the man-made materials found on ground surfaces and roofs in towns, e.g. concrete, asphalt, metal or roof tiles.
LCH-1_5_1: Man-made materials produced from mined earth by mixing components and adding water or heat, e.g. concrete, glass or brick.
LCH-1_5_1_1: Glass used as a surface material, for example on glass roofs or glazed building surfaces.
LCH-1_5_1_2: Fired clay products used on roofs and ground surfaces, e.g. clay roof tiles, ceramic tiles or bricks.
LCH-1_5_1_3: Concrete used as a surface material, e.g. on pavements, car parks or flat roofs.
LCH-1_5_1_4: Cement boards or sheets reinforced with asbestos fibres, often found on older roofs, e.g. corrugated roofing sheets.
LCH-1_5_1_5: Fibre-reinforced cement boards or sheets made without asbestos, used for example as roofing or cladding.
LCH-1_5_2: Surfaces covered with solar panels, e.g. photovoltaic panels on a roof or in a solar park.
LCH-1_5_3: Metal used as a surface material, mainly on roofs, e.g. copper, zinc, aluminium or steel sheeting.
LCH-1_5_3_1: Copper used as a surface material, e.g. a copper roof, often turning green with age.
LCH-1_5_3_2: Zinc used as a surface material, e.g. zinc roof sheeting.
LCH-1_5_3_3: Aluminium used as a surface material, e.g. aluminium roof panels.
LCH-1_5_3_4: Steel used as a surface material, e.g. steel roofing sheets on warehouses or factories.
LCH-1_5_3_5: Iron used as a surface material, e.g. corrugated iron roofing.
LCH-1_5_3_6: Lead used as a surface material, e.g. lead sheeting on roofs.
LCH-1_5_4: Materials made from leftovers of refined crude oil, often mixed with sand or gravel to seal roads and roofs, e.g. asphalt or tar.
LCH-1_5_4_1: Tar, a dark sticky oil-based material used to seal and harden surfaces such as roads or roofs.
LCH-1_5_4_2: Asphalt, the dark oil-based mix with gravel or sand commonly used to pave roads and car parks.
LCH-1_5_4_3: Bitumen, a thick oil-based binder used to waterproof surfaces, e.g. bitumen roofing felt or road surfacing.
LCH-1_5_5: Synthetic materials made industrially by chemical processing, e.g. plastics, rubber and synthetic fibres used on surfaces.
LCH-1_5_5_1: Hard rubber used as a surface material, e.g. rubber flooring on playgrounds or sports areas.
LCH-1_5_5_2: Rigid plastic used as a surface material, e.g. plastic roofing panels.
LCH-1_5_5_3: Thin plastic sheeting covering a surface, e.g. foil over crops or a plastic liner.
LCH-1_5_5_4: Synthetic fibre used as a surface material, e.g. artificial turf on a sports pitch.
LCH-1_5_6: Natural stone materials taken from quarries, riverbeds, beaches and similar sources, used without chemical processing, e.g. gravel or slate.
LCH-1_5_6_1: Natural stone used as a surface material, e.g. cobblestones or stone slabs.
LCH-1_5_6_2: Slate, a natural stone that splits into thin flat layers, commonly used as roofing on older houses.
LCH-1_5_6_3: Loose small stones used on surfaces, e.g. a gravel path or pebble-covered roof.
LCH-1_5_6_4: Sand used as a surface material, e.g. on a sports ground or path.
LCH-1_5_6_5: Ashes or slag, the leftovers from burning or metal smelting, used as a surface material, e.g. on a cinder track.
LCH-1_5_7: Surface materials of plant origin used on roofs or the ground, e.g. wooden shingles or thatch.
LCH-1_5_7_1: Wood used as a surface material, e.g. wooden shingles, decking or boardwalks.
LCH-1_5_7_2: Plant stems or leaves used as a surface material, e.g. a thatched roof of reed or straw.
LCH-1_6: Groups the ways surface materials are laid out on ground or roofs, e.g. a continuous layer, paving stones or overlapping tiles.
LCH-1_6_1: Material laid as one continuous layer with no joints, e.g. an asphalt road surface.
LCH-1_6_2: Paving made of separate pieces fitted tightly together with seams but no gaps, e.g. a paved pedestrian street.
LCH-1_6_3: Paving pieces laid with small gaps so rainwater can soak into the ground, e.g. grass pavers in a car park.
LCH-1_6_4: Paving or roofing laid as tiles, which may partly overlap, e.g. a tiled roof.
LCH-1_7: Groups types of vegetation grown on buildings, mainly on roofs and possibly on walls.
LCH-1_7_1: A roof covered with growing plants, e.g. a green roof on an office building.
LCH-1_7_1_1: A green roof with low plants such as herbs, mosses, lichens or dwarf shrubs.
LCH-1_7_1_2: A green roof with taller woody plants such as trees and bushes, often forming a roof garden.
LCH-1_8: Groups details that describe transport areas, such as types of roads and paths and types of harbours.
LCH-1_8_1: Groups types of roads and paths by their main use, from highways to footpaths and cycle lanes.
LCH-1_8_1_1: Roads built for fast long-distance traffic, e.g. motorways and highways.
LCH-1_8_1_2: An area reserved for people on foot, sometimes bicycles, where motor traffic is banned or limited, e.g. a shopping street.
LCH-1_8_1_3: A footpath or cycle lane running alongside a road, sometimes separated from it by a narrow green strip.
LCH-1_8_1_4: A path shared by walkers and cyclists on its own route, away from roads.
LCH-1_8_1_5: A path or lane reserved for bicycles only, with no pedestrians or cars, e.g. a separate bike lane.
LCH-1_8_1_6: A path meant only for people on foot, e.g. a footpath.
LCH-1_8_1_7: An open, often rectangular or round space in the street network, e.g. a town square or a large roundabout.
LCH-1_8_4: Groups types of port areas where ships and boats dock, load and unload, e.g. cargo ports, marinas and shipyards.
LCH-1_8_4_1: A port where traded goods are shipped in and out, usually with container terminals.
LCH-1_8_4_2: A port where people board and leave ships, e.g. a ferry or cruise terminal.
LCH-1_8_4_3: A port used by fishing boats bringing in their catch from the sea.
LCH-1_8_4_4: A port that serves military ships, e.g. a navy base harbour.
LCH-1_8_4_5: A harbour for yachts and sport boats used for recreation and leisure.
LCH-1_8_4_6: A local harbour not limited to one kind of vessel, serving several purposes at once.
LCH-1_8_4_7: An area by the sea or a river where ships are built, maintained or repaired, either afloat or in a dry dock.
LCH-1_8_4_8: A long structure reaching out from the shore where vessels dock to load, unload or let passengers on and off.
LCH-2: Groups physical properties of the land itself, such as ground that stays permanently frozen.
LCH-2_1: Areas where the ground stays frozen for at least two years in a row, found in polar regions or high mountains.
LCH-3: Groups details describing plants and vegetation, e.g. leaf shape, whether leaves fall, lifespan, growth form and species origin.
LCH-3_1: Groups the basic leaf shapes used to tell trees and shrubs apart, e.g. needle leaves or broad leaves.
LCH-3_1_1: Trees and shrubs with thin, needle-shaped leaves, e.g. pine, spruce or fir.
LCH-3_1_2: Plants with broad, flat leaves, e.g. oak, beech or maple.
LCH-3_1_3: Plants with the large fan- or feather-shaped leaves typical of palms, e.g. palm trees.
LCH-3_1_4: Plants that have no leaves at all, e.g. many cacti that use green stems instead.
LCH-3_2: Groups plants by whether they shed their leaves or needles each season or keep them for several years.
LCH-3_2_1: Plants that keep their leaves or needles for several years, e.g. spruce or holly.
LCH-3_2_2: Plants that lose their leaves or needles at the end of each growing cycle, usually every year, e.g. beech or larch.
LCH-3_2_2_1: Plants that drop their leaves each year to cope with freezing winter temperatures, e.g. oak or birch.
LCH-3_2_2_2: Plants that drop their leaves each year before or during hot summers to avoid drying out.
LCH-3_3: Groups features of the leaf's outer structure, such as how its surface or skin is built.
LCH-3_3_1: Plants with small, hard, leathery or waxy leaves adapted to long dry and hot periods, e.g. olive trees or cork oaks.
LCH-3_4: Groups plants by how long they live, from one season to many years.
LCH-3_4_1: A plant that completes its whole life cycle within one growing season, e.g. many cereals or summer flowers.
LCH-3_4_2: A plant whose life cycle spans two years, flowering and setting seed in the second year.
LCH-3_4_3: A plant that survives unfavourable seasons such as winter and lives more than two years.
LCH-3_4_4: A plant that runs through several life cycles in one growing season and can multiply quickly.
LCH-3_5: Groups plants by where they grow: on land, on other plants, under water or at the water surface.
LCH-3_5_1: Plants growing on solid ground, including wetland plants like reeds that stand in water.
LCH-3_5_2: A plant that grows on another plant for support, taking moisture and nutrients from air, rain or debris rather than its host.
LCH-3_5_3: Water plants living mainly below the surface without reaching it, e.g. algae.
LCH-3_5_4: Water plants that mainly float on the water surface, e.g. water lilies.
LCH-3_6: Groups the overall shapes plants grow into, describing how their stems and branches are arranged.
LCH-3_6_1: A woody plant with one main upright stem, as in a typical tree.
LCH-3_6_2: A woody plant with several stems growing from the ground upward and outward, e.g. bushes and shrubs.
LCH-3_6_3: Plants whose branches or shoots lie on or just above the ground and spread sideways rather than upright.
LCH-3_6_4: Plants growing as a compact mound or thicket with shoots spreading out from the centre, e.g. bamboos, sedges or some grasses.
LCH-3_6_5: Low, compact, pillow-like or mat-forming plants with tightly packed branches, found in alpine and arctic environments.
LCH-3_6_6: Plants that climb on other plants or objects for support because they lack strong stems, e.g. ivy or grapevine.
LCH-3_7: Groups plants by Raunkiaer's system, which classifies them by where their buds survive the unfavourable season, e.g. high above ground or underground.
LCH-3_7_1: A Raunkiaer life form for plants whose resting buds sit well above the ground on woody stems, e.g. trees and tall shrubs.
LCH-3_7_2: A Raunkiaer life form for plants that grow on other plants rather than rooting in the soil.
LCH-3_7_3: A Raunkiaer life form for low plants whose resting buds sit close above the ground, e.g. dwarf shrubs.
LCH-3_7_4: A Raunkiaer life form for plants whose resting buds sit right at the soil surface, e.g. many grasses.
LCH-3_7_5: A Raunkiaer life form for plants whose resting buds survive below ground or under water, e.g. bulbs.
LCH-3_7_6: A Raunkiaer life form for plants that survive the unfavourable season only as seeds, e.g. annual herbs.
LCH-3_7_7: A Raunkiaer life form for plants that live in the air without roots in the soil, taking water and nutrients from the air.
LCH-3_8: Groups the direction vegetation cover is changing in: either recovering naturally or degrading over time.
LCH-3_8_1: Land where vegetation is regrowing on its own through natural succession, e.g. abandoned fields turning into scrub.
LCH-3_8_2: Land where the vegetation cover is getting poorer or thinner over time.
LCH-3_9: Groups plants by their origin relative to where they grow now, e.g. native, introduced, invasive or genetically modified.
LCH-3_9_1: A plant species that has naturally grown in this region for a long time, though not necessarily only here.
LCH-3_9_2: A plant species that is not normally found in this region.
LCH-3_9_3: A plant species found only in this particular region and nowhere else, at any scale from a tiny habitat to a continent.
LCH-3_9_4: A plant from elsewhere that is spreading into a new area, often helped by human transport, and crowding out native plants.
LCH-3_9_5: A plant species gradually moving into a neighbouring area because conditions in its original habitat are changing, e.g. due to climate.
LCH-3_9_6: A plant whose genes have been altered, e.g. crops modified for higher yield or drought resistance.
LCH-3_10: Groups ways to record which plant species are present, following the INSPIRE species distribution standard.
LCH-3_10_1: Records the name of the specific plant species growing in an area.
LCH-3_11: Groups ways to record which plant community grows in an area; still being finalised, possibly following the European Vegetation Survey scheme.
LCH-3_11_1: Records the plant community, meaning a typical group of species growing together, e.g. a beech forest community.
LCH-3_12: Groups details about the natural growing season of wild and local plants. Crop seasons are recorded elsewhere.
LCH-3_12_1: Indicates whether the natural growing season of a plant or plant community is currently under way. Does not cover crop seasons.
LCH-3_13: Measures how much of an area is covered from above by tree or bush crowns, given as a percentage (%).
LCH-4: Groups details that describe water surfaces or relate to water, such as how natural a water body is and how often it holds water.
LCH-4_1: Groups water bodies by how natural they are, from untouched rivers and lakes to fully man-made canals.
LCH-4_1_1: A river or lake in its natural state, with no artificial banks and no dams or weirs controlling its flow.
LCH-4_1_2: A river or lake shaped by man-made structures that hold its banks or control its water level, e.g. most navigable rivers.
LCH-4_1_3: A fully artificial water body that would not exist without people, e.g. a shipping canal or irrigation reservoir.
LCH-4_2: Groups inland waters by how often and how long they hold or carry water, e.g. permanent or seasonal. Not used for sea or tidal areas.
LCH-4_2_1: A riverbed or lake bed that is normally dry, with water flowing only rarely after heavy rain, e.g. a wadi in a desert region.
LCH-4_2_2: Water appears only during or after rain and then stops flowing again, though some seasonal pattern may still be seen, e.g. a stream that runs after storms.
LCH-4_2_3: Water is present for part of every year, usually in the wet or snowmelt season, e.g. a stream that dries up each summer.
LCH-4_2_4: Water is present all year round, even if the level rises and falls, e.g. a large river or permanent lake.
LCH-4_3: Groups descriptions of whether water in a water body flows or stays still, from fast-moving rivers to stagnant ponds.
LCH-4_3_1: Water that keeps moving with a current, so it is constantly renewed and can wear away or deposit ground material, e.g. a river or creek.
LCH-4_3_2: Water that moves so slowly it causes little or no erosion, usually on very flat land, e.g. a canal or drainage ditch.
LCH-4_3_3: Still water with no current at all, e.g. a lake, pond or puddle.
LCH-4_4: Groups classes describing how wet or dry the soil is, from land covered by shallow water to desert soils with almost no moisture.
LCH-4_4_1: Land that is not a water body but is so wet that shallow water covers its surface, e.g. parts of a marsh or bog.
LCH-4_4_2: Soil soaked with water so that nearly all air spaces are filled, often because groundwater is high or rain is frequent.
LCH-4_4_3: Soil that stays wet all year, with water filling many pores but some air still present, often fed by groundwater close to the surface.
LCH-4_4_4: Soil that is wet only during part of the year, for example in a rainy season or after seasonal flooding.
LCH-4_4_5: Soil with a steady, moderate supply of moisture, enough for plants to avoid drought stress; typical of temperate regions with evenly spread rainfall.
LCH-4_4_6: Soil that alternates between rainy and dry spells, with dry periods dominating; water drains away quickly and little is held for plants.
LCH-4_4_7: Soil where hardly any moisture is available to plants through the year, and droughts may last years; only hardy vegetation survives.
LCH-4_4_8: Soil so dry that no vegetation can grow and almost no life is present, as in true deserts.
LCH-4_4_9: Soil moisture typical of a Mediterranean climate, with cool, wet winters and hot, dry summers.
LCH-4_5: Groups the possible origins of the water that makes land wet, such as rain, surface water or groundwater.
LCH-4_5_1: Land whose wetness comes from rainfall.
LCH-4_5_2: Land whose wetness comes from surface water flowing in, e.g. from a nearby river or runoff.
LCH-4_5_3: Land whose wetness comes from groundwater rising up through the soil from below.
LCH-4_6: Groups classes for how salty water or soil is, from salt-saturated brine to practically salt-free rainwater. Usually given in parts per thousand.
LCH-4_6_1: Water that is saturated or nearly saturated with salt, at 50 parts per thousand or more, e.g. the Dead Sea.
LCH-4_6_2: Salty water as found in the oceans and salt lakes, with 30 to 50 parts per thousand of salt, e.g. the Atlantic Ocean.
LCH-4_6_3: Water saltier than fresh water but less salty than the sea (5 to 30 parts per thousand), e.g. estuaries, lagoons or the Baltic Sea.
LCH-4_6_4: Water with very little salt (0.1 to 0.5 parts per thousand), e.g. most rivers and groundwater; drinkable water lies at the low end.
LCH-4_6_5: Water that is practically free of salt, like rain, snow or dew before it picks up other substances.
LCH-4_7: Measures how acidic or alkaline water is, on a scale from 0 (acidic) to 14 (alkaline), where 7 is neutral like pure water.
LCH-4_8: Groups characteristics of coastal areas that are regularly flooded and drained by the tides.
LCH-4_8_1: Records whether a piece of land is affected by the tides, optionally with the typical rise and fall of the water level.
LCH-4_8_2: Measures the height difference between low tide and high tide at a location, in meters.
LCH-4_9: Groups characteristics of groundwater, the water held underground in soil and rock.
LCH-4_9_1: Measures how far below the ground surface the groundwater (water table) lies, in meters.
LCH-4_10: Groups characteristics describing surfaces covered by snow.
LCH-4_10_1: Measures the depth of snow lying on the ground, in meters.
LCH-4_11: Groups characteristics of surfaces covered by ice, on land or water; currently a placeholder for future entries.
LCH-5: Groups information on how people manage and work the land, such as farming methods, cultivation practices and what crops are grown.
LCH-5_1: Groups characteristics of how farmland is managed, including cultivation forms, farming practices, installations, field work and crop types.
LCH-5_1_1: Groups the main forms farmland takes, shaped by the crops grown and how the land is worked: cropland and managed permanent grassland.
LCH-5_1_1_1: Farmland used to plant, grow and harvest crops, covering both fields of annual crops and orchards or vineyards; managed grassland is separate.
LCH-5_1_1_1_1: Fields that are ploughed or prepared for sowing annual crops, often in rotation, e.g. wheat fields; also includes fallow land and rice fields.
LCH-5_1_1_1_2: Land planted with long-lived, mostly woody crops, often in regular rows, e.g. vineyards, olive groves or fruit orchards.
LCH-5_1_1_2: Grassland kept for several years in a row to grow grass or other herbaceous plants for animal feed or energy, e.g. a hay meadow; it is rarely ploughed.
LCH-5_1_2: Groups the overall farming approaches applied to land, such as crop rotation, plantations or agroforestry, including cropping cycles and plant arrangement.
LCH-5_1_2_1: Different crops are grown on the same field in a planned sequence over several years; applies mainly to land with annual crops.
LCH-5_1_2_2: The same crop is grown on a field year after year over a long period, rather than alternating crops.
LCH-5_1_2_3: Large estates growing cash crops in rows using industrialised methods aimed at high yields, e.g. a large fruit plantation with plants tied to wires.
LCH-5_1_2_4: Low-intensity farming, for example traditional orchards of scattered fruit, nut or olive trees, often with grass underneath and valuable for wildlife.
LCH-5_1_2_5: Trees combined with farming on the same land, with livestock grazing or crops grown between scattered trees, e.g. the Spanish dehesa.
LCH-5_1_2_6: Slash-and-burn farming, mainly in the tropics: forest is cleared and burnt, cropped for a few years, then left to regrow before the cycle repeats.
LCH-5_1_2_7: Growing two or more crops together on the same field at the same time to use space better, e.g. a tall nut tree crop with a shade-tolerant crop below.
LCH-5_1_2_8: Small plots of fruit, vegetables and herbs grown mainly for the household's own use rather than for sale.
LCH-5_1_2_9: Rice grown on fields that are flooded for part of the season; the only rice-growing method used in Europe.
LCH-5_1_3: Groups technical installations used on farmland to boost plant growth, raise yields or protect crops, such as greenhouses or protective nets.
LCH-5_1_3_1: Crops grown under permanent glass or mounted plastic, where the farmer controls temperature, light and water, e.g. a tomato greenhouse.
LCH-5_1_3_2: Crops covered by plastic sheeting lying directly on the ground or plants, creating a warm, sheltered microclimate, e.g. early strawberries or asparagus.
LCH-5_1_3_3: Nets stretched over crops, mostly orchards or other permanent crops, to protect them from things like birds or hail.
LCH-5_1_3_4: Fruit trees or shrubs trained flat along a frame by pruning and tying their branches, so they grow in neat lines.
LCH-5_1_3_5: Growing plants without soil, with roots in a nutrient-rich water solution, sometimes supported by an inert material, e.g. hydroponic lettuce.
LCH-5_1_3_6: Indoor growing of crops on several stacked levels, in a multi-storey building or on racks inside a greenhouse.
LCH-5_1_4: Groups the routine field work done to keep farmland fertile and productive, from planting to harvest, such as ploughing, fertilizing and irrigation.
LCH-5_1_4_1: Groups options describing whether a field is ploughed and, if known, in which direction relative to the slope.
LCH-5_1_4_1_1: The field is not ploughed; the soil is left undisturbed rather than being turned over before sowing.
LCH-5_1_4_1_2: The field is ploughed, but the direction of ploughing is not known or not recorded.
LCH-5_1_4_1_3: Furrows run along the slope, following the contour lines, which helps slow water running downhill.
LCH-5_1_4_1_4: Furrows run diagonally across the slope, neither along the contours nor straight downhill.
LCH-5_1_4_1_5: Furrows run straight up and down the slope, the way water would flow downhill.
LCH-5_1_4_2: Groups options for whether and how land is fertilized, i.e. given nutrients from plant residues, manure or chemical products to keep soil fertile.
LCH-5_1_4_2_2: The land is fertilized, but the kind of fertilizer used is not known.
LCH-5_1_4_2_3: Natural fertilizer such as plant material or animal manure spread on or ploughed into the field.
LCH-5_1_4_2_3_1: Animal dung or manure spread on or ploughed into fields as a natural fertilizer.
LCH-5_1_4_2_3_2: Plant material grown on or brought to a field and ploughed in to feed the soil, e.g. a cover crop sown between two main crops.
LCH-5_1_4_2_4: Factory-made fertilizers produced from minerals by industrial chemical processes, e.g. nitrogen fertilizer pellets.
LCH-5_1_4_3: Groups options for whether and how unwanted plants competing with a crop for water, light and nutrients are controlled.
LCH-5_1_4_3_1: No measures are taken against weeds on this land.
LCH-5_1_4_3_2: Weeds are controlled, but the method used is not known.
LCH-5_1_4_3_3: Weeds are controlled physically, e.g. by tilling, or biologically, using their natural enemies.
LCH-5_1_4_3_4: Weeds are controlled with chemicals such as herbicides.
LCH-5_1_4_4: Groups options for whether and how crops are protected from insects or other organisms that damage them and reduce yields.
LCH-5_1_4_4_1: No measures are taken against pests on this land.
LCH-5_1_4_4_2: Pests are controlled, but the method used is not known.
LCH-5_1_4_4_3: Pests are controlled physically, e.g. with traps, or biologically, using their natural enemies.
LCH-5_1_4_4_4: Pests are controlled with chemicals such as pesticides.
LCH-5_1_4_5: Groups options for whether land is artificially watered to help crops grow, and by which method, such as sprinklers or drip lines.
LCH-5_1_4_5_1: The land is not artificially watered; crops depend on natural water only.
LCH-5_1_4_5_2: The land is irrigated, but the watering method is not known.
LCH-5_1_4_5_3: Water flows over the field by gravity, through small channels or furrows between crops or by flooding the whole plot.
LCH-5_1_4_5_4: Water sprayed under pressure over the field like artificial rain, from mobile or fixed sprinklers.
LCH-5_1_4_5_5: A long watering arm rotates around a central point, spraying water in a circle; it creates the round green fields seen from the air.
LCH-5_1_4_5_6: Water delivered drop by drop to each plant through thin perforated tubes on the ground, or as a fine mist from micro-sprayers.
LCH-5_1_4_5_7: Water delivered to plants through perforated tubes or tapes buried underground, at or below root level.
LCH-5_1_4_5_8: Plants are watered by hand, e.g. with a hose or watering can.
LCH-5_1_4_6: Groups the places where irrigation water is taken from, such as wells, reservoirs or rivers.
LCH-5_1_4_6_1: Irrigation water pumped from underground water layers, usually through wells.
LCH-5_1_4_6_2: Irrigation water taken from a stored body of water, e.g. a dammed artificial lake, a natural lake or a rainwater cistern.
LCH-5_1_4_6_3: Irrigation water taken directly from a flowing river, stream or creek.
LCH-5_1_4_7: Groups options for whether and how excess water is removed from farmland through drains or ditches, lowering the groundwater level.
LCH-5_1_4_7_1: No drainage is carried out on this land.
LCH-5_1_4_7_2: The land appears to be drained, but the method is not known.
LCH-5_1_4_7_3: Land drained by long open ditches or trenches into which water seeps from the surrounding ground.
LCH-5_1_4_7_4: Land drained by perforated pipes buried beneath the surface, which collect water and carry it away.
LCH-5_1_4_7_5: Land drained by trenches filled with loose material such as gravel, level with the ground so they can be crossed easily.
LCH-5_1_4_8: Groups information on mowing a piece of land, especially how often it is cut during the year.
LCH-5_1_4_8_1: Groups classes describing how intensively land is mowed, from no mowing to several cuts per year.
LCH-5_1_4_8_1_2: The plot is mowed, but how often is not known.
LCH-5_1_4_8_1_3: Low-intensity mowing: the plot is cut once a year, e.g. a traditional hay meadow.
LCH-5_1_4_8_1_4: The plot is mowed twice a year.
LCH-5_1_4_8_1_5: The plot is mowed more than twice a year.
LCH-5_1_4_8_2: Records how many times per year a piece of land is mowed, given as a count.
LCH-5_1_4_9: Removing bushes and young trees from grassland to stop it turning into scrub or woodland, keeping it open, often for grazing.
LCH-5_1_4_10: Burning off unwanted plants on farmland to control growth; the ashes left behind also enrich the soil.
LCH-5_1_4_11: Spreading lime (calcium carbonate) on land to make the soil less acidic; used mainly in conifer forests but also on farmland.
LCH-5_1_4_12: Selectively cutting branches, twigs, buds or roots to shape plants and improve health or harvest, e.g. trimming fruit trees or vines.
LCH-5_1_4_13: A farm plot temporarily taken out of crop production for one or more seasons to let the soil recover, sometimes as part of a crop rotation.
LCH-5_1_5: Groups the reasons crops are grown, such as for food, animal feed, industry or energy; the same crop can serve different purposes on different fields.
LCH-5_1_5_1: Crops grown as food for people, e.g. vegetables, cereals or fruit, whether eaten fresh or processed. Animal feed crops are not included.
LCH-5_1_5_1_1: Crops grown to harvest cereal grains for human food, e.g. wheat for bread.
LCH-5_1_5_1_2: Crops grown so their whole fruits can be eaten, e.g. apples or table grapes.
LCH-5_1_5_1_3: Crops grown to be pressed, fermented or brewed, e.g. into juice, wine, edible oil or flavour extracts.
LCH-5_1_5_2: Crops grown to feed farm animals, e.g. fodder beet, silage maize or alfalfa.
LCH-5_1_5_2_1: Fodder crops stored after harvest in a silo or sealed plastic-covered pile, where fermentation preserves them as silage for animals.

LCH-5_1_6_1_1_9: Cereal crops not listed separately, e.g. triticale or sorghum.

LCH-5_1_6_3_8_7: Cactus plants grown for their edible fruits, known as prickly pears, common in Mediterranean areas.
LCH-5_1_6_3_8_8: Trees grown for persimmons (kaki), orange fruits that are sweet when fully ripe.
LCH-5_1_6_3_9: Groups tropical perennial plants grown for drinks, spices and flavourings, e.g. coffee, cocoa, vanilla and pepper.
