LCH-5_1_7: Groups the stages a crop passes through during the season, from sowing and germination through flowering and ripening to after harvest.
LCH-5_1_7_1: The stage just after seeds are put in the field, before any sprouts or plant growth can be seen.
LCH-5_1_7_2: The early stage when seeds start to grow and the first sprouts appear.
LCH-5_1_7_3: The stage when sprouts grow into young plants, putting out leaves and shoots, e.g. cereals forming side shoots (tillering).
LCH-5_1_7_4: The stage when crops form heads, ears or flowers, e.g. wheat producing ears.
LCH-5_1_7_5: The stage when crops form fruit or grain and mature, after which the plants begin to age and die back.
LCH-5_1_7_6: A field that has been harvested and left bare, with no crop leftovers and no regrowth of weeds yet.
LCH-5_1_7_7: A harvested field where leftovers remain, e.g. straw, stubble or dropped fruit. It can occur together with resprouting on the field.
LCH-5_1_7_8: A harvested field turning green again as weeds or spilled crop seeds sprout on their own. It can occur together with crop residues.
LCH-5_1_8: Groups descriptions of when in the year crops are grown, e.g. summer or winter season, and how many seasons a field has.
LCH-5_1_8_1: Indicates that a crop is currently growing on the land and its growing season has not yet ended.
LCH-5_1_8_2: Crops sown in spring and grown through the warm months, e.g. maize harvested in late summer or autumn.
LCH-5_1_8_3: Crops sown in autumn that stay in the field over winter, e.g. winter wheat harvested the following summer.
LCH-5_1_8_4: Crops grown continuously throughout the whole year rather than in a single season.
LCH-5_1_8_5: The number of separate crop growing seasons that take place on the same land, typically counted per year.
LCH-5_1_9: Groups the roles a crop can play in a crop rotation, such as main crop, follow-on crop, companion crop or cover crop.
LCH-5_1_9_1: The first and main crop of the year, usually sown after the previous year's harvest, normally giving the highest yield.
LCH-5_1_9_2: A second or third crop sown after the year's main crop is harvested; its yield is usually lower than if sown the previous autumn.
LCH-5_1_9_3: An extra crop grown at the same time alongside the main or secondary crop, e.g. to improve soil or biodiversity, and also harvested.
LCH-5_1_9_4: A follow-on crop grown mainly to protect and enrich the soil, e.g. against erosion, rather than for harvest value.
LCH-5_1_10: Groups overall approaches to farming and the bundle of methods they involve, e.g. conventional or organic farming.
LCH-5_1_10_1: Farming that relies on industrial fertilizers, herbicides, pesticides and heavy machinery to get the highest possible yields.
LCH-5_1_10_2: Farming that avoids industrial fertilizers and pesticides, using natural fertilizers such as green manure and biological or mechanical pest control.
LCH-5_1_11: Groups information on whether land is grazed by livestock and how intensively, following the EU farm subsidy system (IACS).
LCH-5_1_11_1: Groups levels describing how heavily land is grazed by animals, from no grazing to grazing of unknown or low intensity.
LCH-5_1_11_1_1: Land where no grazing by livestock has been observed.
LCH-5_1_11_1_2: Land where livestock graze, but how many animals or how intensively is not known.
LCH-5_1_11_1_3: Low-intensity grazing with two or fewer livestock units per hectare, e.g. a few cattle roaming freely on pasture.
LCH-5_1_11_1_4: Pasture carrying a heavy load of animals, defined here as more than 2 livestock units per hectare, e.g. a field densely stocked with dairy cows.
LCH-5_1_11_2: Measures how many grazing animals, counted in livestock units, are kept on each hectare of a particular plot of land.
LCH-5_1_11_3: Groups the ways grazing is spread over the year, from year-round use of pasture to seasonal, rotational or only occasional grazing.
LCH-5_1_11_3_1: Animals graze the land throughout the whole year rather than only in certain seasons, e.g. hardy sheep kept outdoors in all months.
LCH-5_1_11_3_2: Animals graze the land only during part of the year, e.g. cattle taken to summer pastures in the mountains.
LCH-5_1_11_3_3: Livestock are moved in turns between fenced sections of pasture (paddocks), so each section gets time to regrow before being grazed again.
LCH-5_1_11_3_4: Land that animals graze only now and then, without a regular schedule, e.g. a meadow used for livestock in some years.
LCH-5_1_11_3_5: Grazing that happens without human management, e.g. wild or free-roaming animals feeding on natural vegetation.
LCH-5_1_11_4: Groups the times of day when animals are out grazing: during daytime, at night, or around the clock.
LCH-5_1_11_4_1: Animals are put out to graze during the day and kept in a barn or enclosure overnight.
LCH-5_1_11_4_2: Animals graze only during the night, and are kept elsewhere during the daytime.
LCH-5_1_11_4_3: Animals stay out on the pasture and graze both by day and by night.
LCH-5_1_11_5: Groups the kinds of animals that graze on a piece of land, such as cattle, sheep, goats, horses or poultry.
LCH-5_1_11_5_1: Land grazed by cows, bulls or other cattle, e.g. a pasture used by beef or dairy herds.
LCH-5_1_11_5_2: Land grazed by horses, e.g. a paddock or meadow where horses are kept.
LCH-5_1_11_5_3: Land grazed by deer, e.g. a fenced area where deer are farmed or kept.
LCH-5_1_11_5_4: Land where pigs or wild boars graze and root, e.g. outdoor pig farming in woodland or fields.
LCH-5_1_11_5_5: Land grazed by sheep, e.g. upland pastures or hillsides used for sheep farming.
LCH-5_1_11_5_6: Land grazed by goats, e.g. rough scrubby slopes used for goat herding.
LCH-5_1_11_5_7: Land where chickens, ducks, geese or other farm birds feed outdoors, e.g. a free-range poultry run.
LCH-5_1_11_5_8: Grazing animals not listed separately, e.g. donkeys, llamas or alpacas.
LCH-5_2: Groups the ways woodland is managed: tree ages, species mix, harvesting and replanting methods, and what the wood is used for.
LCH-5_2_1: Describes how tree ages are mixed within a forest plot, which reflects how it has been planted, managed and harvested.
LCH-5_2_1_1: A forest plot where all trees are about the same age, usually because they were planted together, e.g. a uniform spruce plantation.
LCH-5_2_1_2: A forest plot containing trees of different ages growing side by side.
LCH-5_2_1_3: Forest made mostly of self-sown native trees whose ages and species mix come from natural growth, e.g. old woodland in a strict forest reserve.
LCH-5_2_2: Groups forests by roughly how old the trees are at the time of observation, from seedlings to mature trees.
LCH-5_2_2_1: Very young trees in their first years of growth, roughly up to about 5 years old, e.g. a freshly replanted clearing.
LCH-5_2_2_2: Trees in an early growth stage, roughly 5 to 15 years old as a rough guide, no longer seedlings but not yet fully grown.
LCH-5_2_2_3: Fully grown trees, roughly 20 years and older as a guide; a tree counts as mature once it starts producing flowers or fruit.
LCH-5_2_3: Indicates whether a forest plot contains a mixture of tree species or consists mainly of one species.
LCH-5_2_3_1: Forest where several tree species grow together, e.g. oak, beech and hornbeam in the same stand.
LCH-5_2_3_2: Forest made up mostly of a single tree species, whether planted as a monoculture or growing that way naturally, e.g. a pure pine stand.
LCH-5_2_4: Groups the main overall strategies for growing and harvesting woodland, such as coppice, high forest, or a mix of the two.
LCH-5_2_4_1: Traditionally managed, usually broadleaved woodland whose trees are cut back every 15 to 25 years and regrow new shoots from the stumps.
LCH-5_2_4_2: Woodland combining coppice, regularly cut back to the stumps, with taller trees left to grow into high forest above it.
LCH-5_2_4_3: Woodland of tall, straight-stemmed trees grown from seed or planted seedlings, usually forming a closed canopy when mature, e.g. a beech or spruce forest.
LCH-5_2_5: Groups forests by how long trees are grown before they are felled, from very short cycles to continuous forest cover.
LCH-5_2_5_1: Very dense plantings of fast-growing trees, usually willow or poplar, cut every 2 to 5 years and left to resprout from the stumps.
LCH-5_2_5_2: Trees planted and felled once they reach about 10 to 20 cm trunk diameter, typically after 6 to 20 years, often for energy wood.
LCH-5_2_5_3: The most common forest management cycle, where trees are harvested once stands are around 40 to 50 years old or older.
LCH-5_2_5_4: Forest kept permanently wooded by harvesting individual trees rather than clear cutting, usually leaving a mix of species and ages.
LCH-5_2_6: Groups the ways a forest renews itself after harvest or disturbance, either through planting and sowing by people or through natural regrowth.
LCH-5_2_6_1: Forest renewal started by people, who deliberately plant young trees or sow seeds, e.g. replanting saplings after a harvest.
LCH-5_2_6_2: Forest renewal that happens naturally, with trees reproducing from their own seeds and fruits and no human planting involved.
LCH-5_2_6_2_1: Natural forest regrowth where trees spread by dropping or scattering their own seeds, e.g. birch seedlings appearing in a clearing.
LCH-5_2_6_2_2: Natural regrowth of new shoots from roots, branches or a cut or broken stump, e.g. after coppicing.
LCH-5_2_7: Groups care measures applied to forest trees and soil to keep them healthy and growing well, such as thinning, pruning or drainage.
LCH-5_2_7_1: Clearing competing plants such as weeds or unwanted young trees from around seedlings during the first years of a new forest.
LCH-5_2_7_2: Removing some trees from a stand so the best ones get more light, water, nutrients and space to grow.
LCH-5_2_7_3: Selectively cutting off parts of trees, such as branches, buds or roots, to shape growth or remove dead or damaged parts.
LCH-5_2_7_4: Cutting a ring of bark around a tree's trunk, which interrupts its flow of nutrients and causes it to die gradually.
LCH-5_2_7_5: Planting young trees of other species within a single-species forest to make it more mixed, e.g. adding beech to a pine plantation.
LCH-5_2_7_6: Clearing fallen or standing dead trees and branches out of a forest.
LCH-5_2_7_7: Watering forest trees artificially, e.g. to help young plantations through dry periods.
LCH-5_2_7_8: Draining wet forest land with ditches or pipes so that trees can grow better.
LCH-5_2_7_9: Spreading lime on forest soil to reduce its acidity, e.g. in areas affected by acid rain.
LCH-5_2_7_10: A strip cleared of trees and burnable vegetation inside or around a forest, meant to stop or slow the spread of wildfires.
LCH-5_2_8: Groups the common methods of harvesting timber, which in forestry are closely tied to how the forest is then regenerated.
LCH-5_2_8_1: Felling all trees on a plot at once, leaving none standing, e.g. a fully harvested section of plantation awaiting replanting.
LCH-5_2_8_2: Felling mature trees gradually, a few at a time and spread evenly across the plot, so the remaining trees shelter the young growth.
LCH-5_2_8_3: Felling mature trees over several years in scattered groups or patches, creating island-like gaps where new trees grow.
LCH-5_2_8_4: Felling a mature forest step by step in strips, starting at the outer edge of the plot and moving inward year by year.
LCH-5_2_8_5: Harvesting only selected trees that are ready for cutting while leaving the rest to keep growing, which keeps the forest continuously covered.
LCH-5_2_8_6: Repeatedly cutting tree stems close to the ground so new shoots grow from the stump, which are harvested again in later cycles.
LCH-5_2_8_7: Cutting a tree's top a few metres above ground so it sprouts many thin shoots, e.g. for leafy fodder or neatly shaped street trees.
LCH-5_2_9: Groups forests by what their trees are used for: wood, fibre, energy or non-wood products such as cork or resin.
LCH-5_2_9_1: Forests whose main product is wood itself, whether for building material, fuel or fibre for paper.
LCH-5_2_9_1_1: Wood harvested for use as construction material, e.g. for furniture, buildings or bridges.
LCH-5_2_9_1_2: Wood harvested to be burned for energy or turned into charcoal, e.g. firewood.
LCH-5_2_9_1_3: Wood harvested to produce cellulose, the raw material for pulp and paper.
LCH-5_2_9_2: Goods from forests that are of biological origin but are not wood, e.g. cork, resin, rubber, bamboo or Christmas trees.
LCH-5_2_9_2_1: Bark harvested from cork oak trees, used for products such as wine stoppers and insulation boards.
LCH-5_2_9_2_2: Sticky sap collected by tapping a hole into a tree trunk and gathering the resin the tree produces to seal the wound.
LCH-5_2_9_2_3: Milky sap gathered from wounds in the bark of rubber trees, mostly grown on tropical plantations, and used to make natural rubber.
LCH-5_2_9_2_4: Aromatic resin from Boswellia trees, burnt to give off fragrant smoke in religious or ritual ceremonies.
LCH-5_2_9_2_5: Gum-resin from small thorny Commiphora trees, used over the centuries as perfume, incense and medicine.
LCH-5_2_10: Groups forests by their origin and past: untouched primary forest, naturally regrown forest, or forest planted by people.
LCH-5_2_10_1: Forest of native trees that regenerated naturally and shows no clearly visible signs of human activity, e.g. untouched old-growth woodland.
LCH-5_2_10_2: Forest that regrew naturally but shows clear signs of past human activity, e.g. after selective logging, farming or human-caused fires.
LCH-5_2_10_3: Re-establishing forest by planting or sowing on land already used as forest, e.g. replanting seedlings after a clear cut or storm damage.
LCH-5_2_10_4: Creating new forest by planting or sowing trees on land that was not forest before, e.g. on former farmland or grassland.
LCH-5_2_11: Groups forests by the main tree types growing there, listed by their scientific genus name, such as Quercus (oaks) or Pinus (pines).
LCH-5_2_11_1: Firs, evergreen conifers with flat needles and upright cones, e.g. the silver fir.
LCH-5_2_11_2: Maples, broadleaved trees known for their lobed leaves and winged seeds, e.g. the sycamore maple.
LCH-5_2_11_3: Horse chestnuts, broadleaved trees with large hand-shaped leaves and shiny brown conkers.
LCH-5_2_11_4: Alders, broadleaved trees often found along rivers and in wet ground, e.g. the black alder.
LCH-5_2_11_5: Birches, broadleaved trees often recognised by their pale, peeling bark, e.g. the silver birch.
LCH-5_2_11_6: Hornbeams, broadleaved trees with very hard wood, often found in mixed woods and hedges.
LCH-5_2_11_7: Sweet chestnuts, broadleaved trees grown for their edible nuts and durable wood.
LCH-5_2_11_8: Cedars, large evergreen conifers with needles in clusters, e.g. the cedar of Lebanon.
LCH-5_2_11_9: Hazels, small broadleaved trees or shrubs that produce hazelnuts, often coppiced.
LCH-5_2_11_10: Trees of the cypress family, evergreen conifers with scale-like leaves, e.g. cypresses and junipers.
LCH-5_2_11_11: Eucalyptus or gum trees, fast-growing evergreen broadleaved trees originally from Australia and often grown in plantations.
LCH-5_2_11_12: Beeches, broadleaved trees with smooth grey bark that often form dense forests, e.g. the European beech.
LCH-5_2_11_13: Ash trees, broadleaved trees with feathery compound leaves, e.g. the common ash.
LCH-5_2_11_14: Ginkgo, an ancient tree species with fan-shaped leaves, often planted in parks and along streets.
LCH-5_2_11_15: Walnut trees, broadleaved trees grown for their nuts and valuable timber.
LCH-5_2_11_16: Larches, conifers that unusually shed their needles in autumn, e.g. the European larch.
LCH-5_2_11_17: Spruces, evergreen conifers with short needles and hanging cones, e.g. the Norway spruce.
LCH-5_2_11_18: Pines, evergreen conifers with long needles in bundles, e.g. the Scots pine.
LCH-5_2_11_19: Plane trees, large broadleaved trees with flaking patchy bark, common along city streets.
LCH-5_2_11_20: Poplars, fast-growing broadleaved trees, including aspens, often planted for wood or along roads.
LCH-5_2_11_21: Douglas firs, tall fast-growing conifers originally from North America and widely planted for timber.
LCH-5_2_11_22: Oaks, long-lived broadleaved trees that bear acorns, e.g. the pedunculate or cork oak.
LCH-5_2_11_23: Willows, broadleaved trees and shrubs usually growing in wet places, also grown as short-rotation energy crops.
LCH-5_2_11_24: Yews, slow-growing evergreen conifers with dark needles and red berry-like fruits.
LCH-5_2_11_25: Lime or linden trees, broadleaved trees with heart-shaped leaves and fragrant flowers.
LCH-5_2_11_26: Elms, broadleaved trees with rough, uneven leaves, many of which were hit hard by Dutch elm disease.
LCH-5_3: Groups characteristics of land used for industry, mainly how mining is done and which raw materials are extracted.
LCH-5_3_1: Groups the methods used to extract raw materials from the ground, such as open pits, underground mines or fracking.
LCH-5_3_1_1: Extracting materials from a large open hole dug down from the surface, e.g. an open-cast coal mine or quarry.
LCH-5_3_1_2: Extracting materials through tunnels and shafts below the surface, e.g. a deep coal or metal mine.
LCH-5_3_1_3: Extracting materials from beneath water, e.g. dredging sand and gravel from a lake or riverbed.
LCH-5_3_1_4: A site where salt is won from salt water, e.g. shallow evaporation ponds along a coast.
LCH-5_3_1_5: Extracting minerals by dissolving them with liquids pumped into the ground or poured over ore, then collecting the solution, e.g. some salt or uranium mining.
LCH-5_3_1_6: Releasing oil or gas from deep rock by pumping in fluid under high pressure to crack it open.
LCH-5_3_2: Groups the kinds of raw materials taken from mines and extraction sites, from fuels such as coal to metal ores and stone.
LCH-5_3_2_1: Fuels formed from ancient plant and animal remains, extracted from the ground, e.g. coal, crude oil or natural gas.
LCH-5_3_2_1_1: Hard, black, high-energy coal, usually mined deep underground and used for power and steel making.
LCH-5_3_2_1_2: Lignite or brown coal, a soft, lower-grade coal often dug from large open-cast mines.
LCH-5_3_2_1_3: Partly decayed plant material from bogs, dug up and dried for fuel or garden use.
LCH-5_3_2_1_4: Petroleum pumped from underground reservoirs in its raw, unrefined form, e.g. from oil wells.
LCH-5_3_2_1_5: Sand or sandstone soaked with a thick, tar-like oil, mined and processed to obtain petroleum.
LCH-5_3_2_1_6: Rocks containing bitumen or oil-rich material, e.g. oil shale, mined as a source of fuel.
LCH-5_3_2_1_7: Natural gas extracted from underground deposits, mainly used for heating and generating power.
LCH-5_3_2_2: Rocks mined because they contain metals worth extracting, e.g. iron, copper or rare earth ores.
LCH-5_3_2_2_1: Rock rich in iron, mined as the raw material for making iron and steel.
LCH-5_3_2_2_2: Ores of metals other than iron, e.g. copper, zinc, lead, aluminium or gold.
LCH-5_3_2_2_3: Ores of a group of special metals used in electronics, magnets and batteries, e.g. neodymium.
LCH-5_3_2_3: Minerals extracted for uses other than metal, e.g. building stone, gravel, salt or gemstones.
LCH-5_3_2_3_1: Rock, sand, gravel, clay and similar materials dug up mainly for building and construction, e.g. from a gravel pit or quarry.
LCH-5_3_2_3_2: Minerals mined as raw materials for the chemical or fertiliser industries, e.g. potash or salt.
LCH-5_3_2_3_2_1: Rock salt or sea salt extracted from mines, brine or evaporation ponds, used in food, industry and road gritting.
LCH-5_3_2_3_3: Gemstones mined for jewellery or decoration, e.g. diamonds, rubies or amethysts.
LCH-5_3_2_4: Mined or extracted materials that do not fit in the other product groups listed here.
LCH-5_4: Groups ways in which people reshape the ground or install structures on it, e.g. terraces, levelled ski slopes or avalanche barriers.
LCH-5_4_1: Slopes reshaped into a series of level steps, mostly so they can be farmed, e.g. vineyard or rice terraces on a hillside.
LCH-5_4_2: Ground heavily reshaped by earthworks, e.g. steep land levelled out or slopes sculpted for ski pistes.
LCH-5_4_3: Land, usually ski pistes, covered with man-made snow from snow cannons to improve skiing and extend the season.
LCH-5_4_4: Areas where snow is collected in winter and covered with insulating material so it lasts through the summer, e.g. for ski slopes next season.
LCH-5_4_5: Structures that stop avalanches from starting or protect areas against them, e.g. snow fences or barriers on mountain slopes.
LCH-5_5: Groups legal rules and restrictions on how land may be used or entered, such as protected areas and access limits.
LCH-5_5_1: Groups land by who is allowed to enter it, from open public access to military-only zones.
LCH-5_5_1_1: Land open to the general public, where anyone may enter, e.g. a public park or common land.
LCH-5_5_1_2: Land that both civilians and the military may use and enter, e.g. a shared training ground with public paths.
LCH-5_5_1_3: Land closed to access for a limited time, e.g. after a severe natural disaster or a contamination event.
LCH-5_5_1_4: Land only the military may enter, with others kept out or allowed in only by special permission, e.g. a military base.
LCH-5_5_2: Groups the kinds of legal protection status an area can have, e.g. nature reserves, national parks or Natura 2000 sites.
LCH-5_5_2_1: Land under strict legal nature protection, where many activities such as farming, building or lighting fires are forbidden.
LCH-5_5_2_2: Protected land where activities like farming and forestry are allowed to a degree, but the look of the landscape must be preserved.
LCH-5_5_2_3: Areas listed under European law as part of the Natura 2000 network of protected sites for nature.
LCH-5_5_2_4: Areas with strict access limits to protect birds, either all year or during the breeding season.
LCH-5_5_2_5: Areas designated by UNESCO to manage nature and human culture together, often with a strictly protected core and less restricted outer zones.
LCH-5_5_2_6: UNESCO-designated areas with internationally important geology, managed for protection, education and sustainable development.
LCH-5_5_2_7: A larger area run by an authority mainly to conserve nature, often combined with recreation and visitor facilities.
LCH-5_5_2_8: Protected areas with a legal status not covered by the other types listed here.
LCH-6: Groups characteristics describing the current state or condition of a piece of land and, if it is damaged, the reason why.
LCH-6_1: Groups labels describing the state a piece of land is in regarding its use, e.g. under construction, out of use or abandoned.
LCH-6_1_1: Land being turned into man-made surfaces, e.g. a building site with excavations or earthworks whose final use is already decided.
LCH-6_1_2: Land that is not used and shows no recognisable traces of ever having been used by people.
LCH-6_1_3: Land that is temporarily not used but will probably be used again, e.g. a factory site on hold.
LCH-6_1_4: Land no longer in use that cannot serve its original purpose without major repair, e.g. a derelict industrial site.
LCH-6_1_5: Land from which trees or shrubs have recently been removed, e.g. a freshly felled forest plot.
LCH-6_1_6: Marks objects that are no longer intact or usable because they were destroyed or collapsed, mostly buildings, structures or utilities, e.g. a building left in ruins.
LCH-6_1_7: Areas being deliberately returned to a natural or semi-natural state, e.g. by removing paving, cleaning up polluted ground, sowing plants or restoring natural soil moisture.
LCH-6_2: Groups the possible causes of damage to an area, from natural hazards such as floods or earthquakes to human-made harm such as pollution or demolition.
LCH-6_2_1: Damage caused by processes of the solid earth or of water, e.g. earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, landslides or floods.
LCH-6_2_1_1: Damage from a long, powerful wave in the sea or a large lake that reaches land, e.g. one set off by an undersea earthquake or a landslide into a lake.
LCH-6_2_1_2: Damage from a volcano releasing hot magma, ash and gases, including directly linked effects such as ash fall, explosions and fast-moving hot volcanic flows.
LCH-6_2_1_3: Damage from ground shaking when stress in the Earth's crust is suddenly released, along with direct effects such as soil turning soft and losing strength.
LCH-6_2_1_4: Damage from the ground sinking or caving in, mainly downward movement when weathered or compacted rock or soil can no longer carry its own weight.
LCH-6_2_1_5: Damage from soil, rock and other material moving downhill when a slope fails, e.g. slides, rock falls or debris flows.
LCH-6_2_1_6: Damage from a large mass of snow sliding rapidly down a slope, often carrying trees and rocks along its path.
LCH-6_2_1_7: Damage from water covering land that is normally dry, e.g. a river overflowing its banks, a flash flood or a tidal flood.
LCH-6_2_2: Groups damage caused by weather or by longer-term climate conditions, e.g. droughts, heat waves, storms or lightning.
LCH-6_2_2_1: Damage from a long, widespread period with less water than usual due to climate variability; not the same as a naturally dry climate.
LCH-6_2_2_2: Damage from unusually hot or cold spells lasting longer than normal, e.g. heat waves or cold waves with frost.
LCH-6_2_2_3: Damage from violent, high-speed winds such as tornadoes or hurricanes, e.g. trees blown over in a forest.
LCH-6_2_2_4: Damage from lightning strikes, the electrical discharges usually linked to thunderclouds but which can also happen in dry conditions.
LCH-6_2_2_5: Damage from seawater pushed onto land by a storm or a sudden change in air pressure, e.g. during a hurricane; treated separately from other floods.
LCH-6_2_3: Groups damage caused by fire breaking out and spreading, whether above ground in vegetation or below the surface.
LCH-6_2_3_1: Damage from fire spreading over vegetated land, such as forests and other wooded land, e.g. a summer wildfire; planned controlled burns are excluded.
LCH-6_2_3_2: Damage from fire burning below the ground surface, typically in soils rich in peat or coal, e.g. a smouldering peat fire.
LCH-6_2_4: Groups damage caused by living organisms or what they produce, e.g. insect pests, diseases or grazing animals.
LCH-6_2_4_1: Damage caused by large numbers of insects attacking plants or trees, e.g. bark beetles killing patches of forest.
LCH-6_2_4_2: Damage caused by mould or similar fungi spreading on plants, materials or buildings.
LCH-6_2_4_3: Harm from a disease outbreak that spreads quickly among people, animals or plants in an area.
LCH-6_2_4_4: Biological substances, such as pollen, that can cause allergic reactions in many people in an area.
LCH-6_2_4_5: Vegetation damaged by animals biting off plant parts or grazing so heavily, even tearing out roots, that plants cannot recover.
LCH-6_2_4_6: Damage to plant cover caused by animals repeatedly walking over it, e.g. bare paths worn by livestock.
LCH-6_2_5: Groups damage that originates from outer space, such as meteorite impacts or radiation.
LCH-6_2_5_1: Damage caused by solid material from outer space striking the Earth's surface, e.g. a crater left by a meteorite.
LCH-6_2_5_2: Damage linked to disturbances of the Earth's magnetic field caused from space, e.g. during strong solar storms.
LCH-6_2_5_3: Damage from radiation coming from outer space, such as ultraviolet light or gamma rays.
LCH-6_2_6: Groups damage caused by harmful substances in the ground, water or air, e.g. chemicals, oil, radioactivity or plastic.
LCH-6_2_6_1: Land or water polluted by radioactive material, e.g. areas affected by a nuclear accident.
LCH-6_2_6_2: Land or water polluted by harmful chemicals or toxic substances, e.g. waste from industrial sites.
LCH-6_2_6_3: Soil damaged by a build-up of salts, which harms plant growth and can make farmland less productive.
LCH-6_2_6_4: Land or water polluted by oil, e.g. after a pipeline leak or an oil spill on a coast.
LCH-6_2_6_5: Areas contaminated by military ammunition or industrial explosives, e.g. a former firing range with unexploded shells.
LCH-6_2_6_6: Areas polluted by plastic, whether large pieces of litter or tiny microplastic particles.
LCH-6_2_7: Groups damage to buildings and other structures caused by people, either on purpose or by accident, e.g. demolition or neglect.
LCH-6_2_7_1: Damage from structures slowly falling apart over time, e.g. an abandoned building crumbling through lack of maintenance.
LCH-6_2_7_2: Damage from structures being deliberately torn down or blown up, or from an explosion.
LCH-6_3: Groups slow processes that wear down or degrade land over time, e.g. soil erosion, desertification or melting glaciers.
LCH-6_3_1: Loss of tree cover, whether from natural causes or human activity, e.g. drought, storms, clear-cutting or soil erosion.
LCH-6_3_2: Loss of fertile topsoil carried away by wind, flowing water or gravity, e.g. soil washed off a field after heavy rain.
LCH-6_3_3: Vegetated land gradually turning into desert, typically after years of low rainfall combined with human or animal pressure such as soil salinization.
LCH-6_3_4: Areas where glaciers have shrunk in size or thickness by melting as average temperatures rise.
LCH-7: Groups characteristics describing where a piece of land lies geographically, e.g. its habitat, altitude zone, climate, landscape setting and terrain.
LCH-7_1: Groups types of natural or human-shaped surroundings in which people, animals and plants live, largely following the European EUNIS habitat types.
LCH-7_1_1: Habitats in the sea, from shallow coastal waters to the deep ocean floor, e.g. seagrass meadows or reefs.
LCH-7_1_2: Habitats along the coast where land meets sea, e.g. beaches, dunes, sea cliffs and shingle shores.
LCH-7_1_3: Habitats in and around freshwater on land, e.g. lakes, ponds, rivers and streams.
LCH-7_1_4: Wet habitats with waterlogged, often peaty ground, e.g. raised bogs or fens fed by groundwater.
LCH-7_1_5: Open habitats where grasses, herbs, mosses or lichens dominate rather than trees or shrubs, e.g. meadows and pastures.
LCH-7_1_6: Habitats dominated by low woody plants or cold-adapted vegetation, e.g. heather moors, shrubland or Arctic tundra.
LCH-7_1_7: Habitats dominated by trees, from dense forests to more open wooded land, e.g. beech forests or pine woodland.
LCH-7_1_8: Inland habitats with bare or very sparse plant cover, e.g. rock outcrops, screes, sand areas or snowfields.
LCH-7_1_9: Habitats created and kept up by farming, gardening or domestic use, e.g. arable fields, orchards or gardens.
LCH-7_1_10: Habitats made or heavily shaped by human construction and industry, e.g. buildings, roads, quarries or waste tips.
LCH-7_1_11: Areas made up of several different habitat types closely mixed together and treated as one unit, e.g. a river delta.
LCH-7_1_12: Shallow coastal body of water separated from the sea by a barrier such as a sandbar, often with brackish water.
LCH-7_1_13: The wide mouth of a river where freshwater mixes with seawater and tides reach inland.
LCH-7_1_14: A narrow arm of the sea reaching into the land, e.g. a long, steep-sided fjord carved by glaciers.
LCH-7_1_15: Low coastal land covered by salt-tolerant plants and regularly flooded by seawater at high tide.
LCH-7_1_16: Flat stretches of mud or sand that are covered by the sea at high tide and exposed at low tide, e.g. mudflats.
LCH-7_2: Groups altitude bands in mountain regions, where temperature, moisture and vegetation change step by step as height increases.
LCH-7_2_1: Lowland of flat, plain areas with the usual temperatures of the local climate; ideal ground for farming and settlements.
LCH-7_2_2: Hilly land with gently rolling terrain, usually forming the upper limit for vineyards; also called the colline zone.
LCH-7_2_3: Zone with more pronounced relief, valleys and mid-height peaks, where growing crops is rare if it happens at all.
LCH-7_2_4: Clearly cooler zone at the peaks of middle mountain ranges, forming the transition towards the high mountains.
LCH-7_2_5: Upper limit of broadleaved forest where conifers dominate; places here are only inhabited seasonally.
LCH-7_2_6: Transition zone at the upper edge of forests, where scattered trees give way to dwarf pines.
LCH-7_2_7: Zone between the tree line and the snow line, where vegetation is limited to low herbs, grasses and dwarf shrubs, e.g. alpine meadows.
LCH-7_2_8: Highest altitude zone, covered by snow or ice for all or most of the year, where glaciers form and plants are essentially absent.
LCH-7_3: Groups descriptions of the wider setting a piece of land sits in, e.g. urban, rural, coastal or mountain surroundings, whose borders are often fuzzy.
LCH-7_3_1: Land far enough from the coast that it is no longer directly influenced by the sea; the opposite of a coastal setting.
LCH-7_3_2: Land close to the seashore, where nearness to the sea shapes things like ports, towns, industry and tourism.
LCH-7_3_3: Land on an island, influenced by the surrounding sea and by its transport links to the mainland; an island can itself have inland and coastal parts.
LCH-7_3_4: Open sea far from any coastline, from the edge of the continental shelf out to deep-sea areas.
LCH-7_3_5: Setting of cities and their suburbs, where built-up areas and transport networks dominate the landscape and many people live.
LCH-7_3_6: Countryside dominated by farmland or forest, where villages exist but large cities are absent and population density is medium to low.
LCH-7_3_7: Land along riverbanks, generally flat and exposed to changing water levels and floods, often with moisture-loving plants such as willows.
LCH-7_3_8: Land shaped by mountains, including the valleys between them, with steep terrain and several climate and vegetation zones.
LCH-7_4: Groups the shape of the land surface, e.g. a valley, dune or plateau; currently a placeholder where the landform is written as free text.
LCH-7_4_1: A free-text note naming the landform found at a place, e.g. 'moraine' or 'river terrace', since no fixed list of landforms exists yet.
LCH-7_5: Groups the bands along a shoreline, at the sea, a lake or a river, sorted by how often they are under water.
LCH-7_5_1: Strip above the shoreline that water does not reach directly; only high groundwater and moist, sometimes salty soil affect it, plus rare extreme storm surges.
LCH-7_5_2: Splash and spray zone just above the waterline, rarely covered by water but wetted by spray from waves; flooded only during storms or floods.
LCH-7_5_3: Zone between low and high water, regularly covered and uncovered by tides on coasts or by changing water levels along rivers and lakes.
LCH-7_5_4: Zone below the low-water line that is normally always under water, on coasts as well as in rivers and lakes; also called subtidal.
LCH-7_6: Groups broad climate zones of the world, useful e.g. for noting which climate a crop or plant type naturally belongs to.
LCH-7_6_1: Warm climate zone near the equator, hot all year round, e.g. where rainforests or banana plantations are found.
LCH-7_6_2: Climate zone between the tropics and the temperate zone, with hot summers and mild winters, e.g. around the Mediterranean.
LCH-7_6_3: Climate zone of moderate temperatures with clear seasons, such as most of central and western Europe.
LCH-7_6_4: Cold climate zone near and around the poles, with long winters and short, cool summers, e.g. the Arctic.
LCH-7_7: Groups measurable properties of the ground surface's shape, such as its height, steepness and the direction it faces.
LCH-7_7_1: Groups measured values describing terrain at a point, namely elevation, slope and aspect, usually stored as grid (raster) data.
LCH-7_7_1_1: Height of the ground above sea level, measured in meters.
LCH-7_7_1_2: How steep the ground rises, i.e. the slope angle, recorded in degrees.
LCH-7_7_1_3: Compass direction a slope faces, given in degrees from 0 to 360, where 0 is north, 90 east, 180 south and 270 west.
LCH-8: Groups characteristics describing how things are arranged inside a piece of land, e.g. mixed or uniform patterns, hedgerows or road networks.
LCH-8_1: Groups two-dimensional patterns showing how different land cover elements are spread out and relate to each other within an area.
LCH-8_1_1: Area that is uniform throughout, with every spot of the same kind and even texture, e.g. the lawn of a football pitch.
LCH-8_1_2: Area where several different features are mixed together fairly evenly, giving an uneven, patchy texture, e.g. trees and shrubs intermingled.
LCH-8_1_3: Area made up of distinct patches, each uniform in itself but clearly different from its neighbours, e.g. a patchwork of small fields.
LCH-8_1_4: A feature that appears only here and there, unevenly spread and not dominant, e.g. scattered trees in a pasture.
LCH-8_1_5: Objects arranged at regular, even distances from each other, e.g. houses in a planned housing estate or trees in an orchard.
LCH-8_2: Groups narrow linear landscape features, too small to map one by one, that still shape an area's character, e.g. hedgerows or stone walls.
LCH-8_2_1: A plot of land surrounded by or divided by several hedgerows, giving it a sub-divided look; mostly found in farming areas.
LCH-8_2_2: A plot of land surrounded by or containing several lines of trees, e.g. windbreaks in the countryside or tree-lined avenues in towns.
LCH-8_2_3: A plot of land surrounded by or containing several traditional dry stone walls, typical of old farming landscapes.
LCH-8_3: Groups networks of linear technical structures that run through an area and shape its look, e.g. small roads, ditches, fences or pipelines.
LCH-8_3_1: Shows that an area contains a recognisable network of roads or railways, even if their exact location is not known.
LCH-8_3_2: Shows that an area contains one pipeline or a network of them, even if their exact location is not known.
LCH-8_4: Groups the vertical position of an object relative to the ground: on the surface, raised above it, or below it.
LCH-8_4_1: An object located directly on the ground surface, e.g. a road at street level.
LCH-8_4_2: An object raised above the ground or hanging over it, e.g. a bridge, an elevated railway or overhead power lines.
LCH-8_4_3: An object located below the ground surface, e.g. a tunnel, subway line or buried pipe.
LCH-9: Groups measurements of objects, such as size, how often they occur and when or how long things happen; always used together with another class.
LCH-9_1: Groups size measurements for objects, such as area, length, width, height and share of an area covered.
LCH-9_1_1: Size of an object's area in square meters, recorded as a from/to range; for an exact value both ends are the same.
LCH-9_1_1_1: Lower end of the range for an object's area, in square meters.
LCH-9_1_1_2: Upper end of the range for an object's area, in square meters.
LCH-9_1_2: Length of an object in meters, recorded as a from/to range; for an exact value both ends are the same.
LCH-9_1_2_1: Lower end of the range for an object's length, in meters.
LCH-9_1_2_2: Upper end of the range for an object's length, in meters.
LCH-9_1_3: Width of an object in meters, recorded as a from/to range; for an exact value both ends are the same.
LCH-9_1_3_1: Lower end of the range for an object's width, in meters.
LCH-9_1_3_2: Upper end of the range for an object's width, in meters.
LCH-9_1_4: How tall an object stands above the ground (not height above sea level), in meters, recorded as a from/to range.
LCH-9_1_4_1: Lower end of the range for an object's height above ground, in meters.
LCH-9_1_4_2: Upper end of the range for an object's height above ground, in meters.
LCH-9_1_5: Share of a larger area taken up by a given cover or use, as a percentage range, e.g. trees covering 30 to 40% of a park.
LCH-9_1_5_1: Lower end of the range for the percentage of an area covered by a given cover or use, in %.
LCH-9_1_5_2: Upper end of the range for the percentage of an area covered by a given cover or use, in %.
LCH-9_2: Groups ways of saying how many or how much of something is present in an area, as a percentage, a count or simply as present.
LCH-9_2_1: Share of certain objects among all distinct objects in an area, given as a percentage range, e.g. the proportion of buildings that are houses.
LCH-9_2_1_1: Lower end of the range for the percentage share of certain objects among all objects in an area, in %.
LCH-9_2_1_2: Upper end of the range for the percentage share of certain objects among all objects in an area, in %.
LCH-9_2_2: Absolute number of certain objects found in an area, recorded as a from/to range, e.g. how many wind turbines stand in a field.
LCH-9_2_2_1: Lower end of the range for how many of the objects occur in the area, as a plain count.
LCH-9_2_2_2: Upper end of the range for how many of the objects occur in the area, as a plain count.
LCH-9_2_3: Simply records that something is present in an area when its exact number or amount cannot be given.
LCH-9_3: Groups time information about things in an area, such as the date of an event, how long something lasts or how often it recurs.
LCH-9_3_1: Date of a sudden, short event that changes the landscape, e.g. a storm, given as the day number counted from 1 January.
LCH-9_3_1_1: Start of a short time window in which a sudden event happened, given as day of the year.
LCH-9_3_1_2: End of a short time window in which a sudden event happened, given as day of the year.
LCH-9_3_2: How long a situation lasts, counted in days, e.g. a crop's growing cycle, a construction site or a flood.
LCH-9_3_2_1: Lower end of the range for how long a situation lasts, in days.
LCH-9_3_2_2: Upper end of the range for how long a situation lasts, in days.
LCH-9_3_3: A span of time bounded by an explicit start date and end date, e.g. the months a field lies fallow.
LCH-9_3_3_1: First day of a period, given as the day number of the year, from 1 for 1 January to 365 for 31 December.
LCH-9_3_3_1_1: Earliest possible start of a period, given as day of the year; used when the exact start date is uncertain.
LCH-9_3_3_1_2: Latest possible start of a period, given as day of the year; used when the exact start date is uncertain.
LCH-9_3_3_2: Last day of a period, given as the day number of the year counted from 1 January.
LCH-9_3_3_2_1: Earliest possible end of a period, given as day of the year; used when the exact end date is uncertain.
LCH-9_3_3_2_2: Latest possible end of a period, given as day of the year; used when the exact end date is uncertain.
LCH-9_3_4: How many times per year something changes or repeats, e.g. how often a meadow is mowed.
LCH-9_3_4_1: Lower end of the range for how many times per year something recurs, as a plain count.
LCH-9_3_4_2: Upper end of the range for how many times per year something recurs, as a plain count.
